Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) and his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (jointly the Appellants) are citizens of Iran, and they are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting their claims for refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) and his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (jointly the Appellants) are citizens of Iran, and they are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting their claims for refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The Appellant submitted documents for consideration as new evidence by the RAD pursuant to subsection 110(4) of IRPA. The Appellants also request a hearing before the RAD.
The Appellants request that the RAD allow the appeal and remit the matter for redetermination by a differently constituted panel.
Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, the RAD remits the matter back to the RPD for redetermination by a differently-constituted panel.
This appeal is allowed.

The Appellants alleged before the RPD that the Appellant is a physician from Afghanistan who fled to Iran in 1981. He married the female Appellant, an Iranian, and they have five children who all fled Iran to Canada, the United States or Europe. In mid-1992 the regime destroyed houses of poor, and a young girl died causing a protest brutally suppressed by the regime resulting in many deaths, injuries and or imprisonments. The Appellant treated many injured and spoke out about the actions of the regime and was told to report to the Sepah. While being interrogated, his hand was hit with such force that the injury required surgery when released. He also lost his job at the local hospital and was forced to work at local charity clinics. Around 1990 he became friends with Colonel XXXX, who helped the Appellant obtain Iranian citizenship and birth certificates, and obtain his medical card in order to enable him to open his own clinic.

Before the 2009 elections, he rented out some office space to a pro-Mousavi candidate to be used as a campaign office for about 15 days. As a result, he was harassed by the local regime and Hezbollah for supporting Mousavi. In late 2011, the claimant and his wife visited their son in Canada and were detained and questioned extensively upon return in Iran. The Appellant was called to the Intelligence office for interrogation about his children living abroad. They accused him that he was in touch with foreign government agents and anti-revolutionary elements and was told not to leave the city without notifying authorities.

His friend, the Colonel, told the Appellants to hide. They eventually left Iran with the help of the Colonel on XXXX XXXX, 2013. After their arrival in Canada, they found out that their home was searched, his housekeeper was detained, his secretary and nurse had been interrogated and the clinic was shut down. They claimed protection in September 2013 and their claims were heard on November 5, 2013. The RPD, in a written decision dated December 5, 2013, found that the Appellants are not credible, and found that they are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of Canada's protection. Grounds for Appeal:

The Appellant's issues are listed below: * What is the Standard of Review? * Did the Board err in its credibility assessment? * Did the Board err by ignoring evidence? * Did the Board err in its analysis of the Appellants' failure to claim elsewhere? * Did the Board err in its analysis of delay in departure? New Evidence:

The Appellants provided the following on appeal: * Presidential Elections and Nuclear Policy in Iran. Arms Control Association, June 2013; * Hamid Ghassemi-Shall's Waking Nightmare Inside an Iranian Jail. MacLeans, November 17, 2013; * Travel Advisory - Iran. Government of Canada, November 29, 2013

In order for the RAD to consider these as new evidence, subsection 110(4) of the Act provides direction and reads as follows: On appeal, the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

In considering the statutory provisions of Section 110(4), the RAD first considered whether the evidence arose after the rejection of the Appellants' refugee claims? Here, the RAD may consider whether the evidence is capable of proving the current state of affairs in the country of feared persecution, or an event that occurred or a circumstance that arose after the rejection of the refugee claim.1 If the evidence is capable of proving an event that occurred or circumstances that arose after the RPD hearing, then the evidence must be considered, and the RAD will proceed to assess the credibility, relevance, and materiality of the document.2 The RAD will consider not only the date on which the document came into existence but the timing of the event or circumstance which the document seeks to prove.3 Subsection 110(4) contemplates the evidence that arose only after the rejection of the Appellant's claim. Where a document arose after the hearing but before the rejection of the refugee claim, the RAD is to consider whether the Appellant could have reasonably presented the document to the RPD by way of a post-hearing submission.

Second, if the RAD finds that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the Appellants' refugee claim, it must consider the next factor in Section 110(4). If the evidence is capable of proving only an event that occurred or circumstances that arose prior to the rejection, has the Appellant established that the evidence was not reasonably available for presentation to the RPD before it rejected the claim,4 or that it proves a fact that was unknown to him/her at the time of the hearing?5 If so, the RAD will proceed to assess the credibility, relevance, and materiality of the documents.

Third, if the RAD finds that the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the Appellant's refugee claim and that it was reasonably available at the time of the rejection, it must consider the final part of the Section 110(4) test, i.e. could the Appellant reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented the evidence prior to the rejection of his refugee claim? If so, the evidence need not be considered.6 If the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected to present the evidence to the RPD, the RAD will proceed to assess the credibility, relevance, and materiality of the document.

However, in this case, these documents do not meet the express statutory conditions of the Act despite the Appellant's submission regarding the first document that states: "The article was not submitted into evidence prior to the hearing as it was impossible to anticipate that the Member would disbelieve the narrow issue that the Appellant would provide support to Mousavi supporters." The Act does not have the provision to accommodate the Appellants who choose to withhold the evidence that could have been provided. These documents may be relevant and material but they have to first meet the statutory conditions of the Act. However, these documents are not capable of proving the events surrounding the Appellant. Moreover, the Appellant was rejected at the hearing and therefore it would be reasonable for him to provide documents in support of the claim.

Since there are no new documents accepted into evidence, the hearing will be conducted on the basis of the record as well as the Appellant's memorandum. Since no new evidence is accepted, the request for the hearing pursuant to subsection 110 (6) is denied. Role of the RAD

The Appellant submits, under the heading the Standard of Review, that the RAD owes no deference to the findings of the RPD. The jurisprudence on the role of the RAD is still evolving, however the court's direction in Huruglica7 seems to be the widely accepted and therefore I will take guidance from Huruglica,8 where the court stated the following: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision. [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is a "palpable and overriding error." Merits of Claim

The Appellant's issues may be rephrased as - did the RPD err in its credibility determination. The Appellant submits that the RPD erred by ignoring or by misconstruing the documentary evidence before it and/or relying heavily on implausibilities and the panel's own opinions as to how people would act if they were afraid.

The Appellant submits that the RPD accepted that the Appellant's hand was crushed by the authorities while interrogating him, however the RPD found his actions to continue to speak out against the regime after this event were "unreasonable in the face of his testimony that he was very afraid." I agree with the Appellant that many people "continue to resist an abusive regime after having himself been abused by them as a physician for the disadvantaged." Thus, I find that the RPD's negative credibility inference drawn from this example is based on implausibility and not supported by fact. Thus, I agree with the Appellant that the RPD panel's finding is based on how the RPD panel expects people to act under certain circumstances.

Similarly, I find that the RPD's negative credibility inference drawn from the fact that the Appellant would rent out a part of his office space to a political opponent during the 2009 elections is not based on fact but on implausibility finding by the RPD. The Appellant provided examples of the millions of people who were mistreated during the 2009 elections. In this particular case, the Appellant also testified that he needed the extra money by renting out the space.

The RPD also made a negative credibility inference from the fact that the Appellant's friend and benefactor, Colonel XXXX, would refuse to speak up on his behalf or write a letter in support of the Appellant despite the fact that he arranged for the Appellant to leave Iran. The RPD found "that providing a letter to the claimant to assist him in his refugee claim is a relatively small request compared to those made previously by the claimant" and drew a negative credibility inference. I find that this again is not supported by evidence. The Appellant testified at the hearing that if the Colonel had been discovered, he would have been executed; which is confirmed by the documentary evidence. The Appellant also submits that the Colonel had made the Appellant promise not to mention his name but, in order to explain his case, he was forced to do so.

I agree with the Appellant that "Repeated throughout the case at bar, the Board simply relied on subjective implausibility findings without any reference to the evidence before it." The Appellant supported his submissions with appropriate jurisprudence that "in Valtchev,9 the Federal Court held that the Board may make adverse credibility findings based on implausibility but only if such inferences are reasonable. The Court stated that implausibility findings should only be made where the documentary evidence demonstrates that the events in question could not have happened. The Court cautions decision-makers not to judge different cultures and actions from a Canadian paradigm." Moreover in Adawi,10 the court stated: [11] An allegation may thus be found to be implausible when it does not make sense in light of the evidence before the Board or when (to borrow the language of Justice Muldoon in Vatchev) it is "outside the realm of what reasonably could be expected." In addition, this Court has held that the Board should provide "a reliable and verifiable evidentiary base against which the plausibility of the Applicants' evidence might be judged," otherwise a plausibility determination may be nothing more than "unfounded speculation" (Gjelaj v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 37 (CanLII), 2010 FC 37 at para 4, [2010] FCJ No 31; see also Cao v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 694 (CanLII), 2012 FC 694 at para 20, [2012] FCJ No 885 [Cao]).

In this case, the RPD did not support its implausibility findings by reliable and verifiable evidence and did not persuade the RAD that the Appellant's testimony was outside the realm of what reasonably could be expected.

In addition, the Appellant submits that the RPD failed to consider documentary evidence before it; in particular, the RPD "ignored the Appellant's son's sworn affidavit regarding events in Iran and the role of Colonel XXXX, whom the family knew;" and letters from the Appellants' children living in the Netherlands, Germany and the USA. These documents describe in detail how the Colonel helped the family and the circumstances under which his help was essential and why the Colonel helped the family. Yet, the RPD makes no reference to any of these letters in the reasons.

In Orgona,11 the court stated: "Even though it is not necessary to refer to all of the documentary evidence before it, when evidence, which supports the applicants' position is not referred to, and when other documentary evidence is selectively relied upon, the tribunal, in my opinion, errs in law by ignoring relevant evidence."

There is a presumption that the RPD has considered all of the evidence before it and the RPD does not have to list and analyse each and every document that was submitted as evidence. However, that presumption can be rebutted. The caselaw is clear that a decision maker is required to address documentary evidence that goes to the heart of the matter. The Appellant appropriately cites Ozdemir,12 where the court stated "The more relevant the contradictory evidence, the greater the duty of the decision-maker to specifically reference it."

In this case, a review of the reasons and transcript of the hearing shows that, in its credibility determination, the RPD did not specifically refer to the documents mentioned above that address some of the key elements of the claim and thus go to merits of the claim. Thus, the RPD, by its failure to consider these documents, erred.
In this case, a review of the reasons and transcript of the hearing shows that, in its credibility determination, the RPD did not specifically refer to documents that have potential probative value.

I also note that the RPD made no reference to section 97 risks and did not put its mind to address this considering the risks to the Appellant, even if there was no nexus to the Convention. The issue of risks under s. 97(1) should have emerged perceptibly given the country conditions in Iran. The RPD made no finding on section 97. There is no indication that the Appellant was not making a claim under section 97 as well as section 96, therefore he was entitled to such a finding. This is an error by the RPD.

For all the foregoing reasons, I find that the RPD erred in its credibility findings by not considering several documents in evidence and by its heavy reliance on implausibility findings. Therefore, the RPD's decision is not supportable. I also find that the RPD erred by not considering the risk pursuant to section 97 of the Act.

I am unable to make a determination as to whether the Appellants are Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under paragraph 111(1)(a) or (b) without hearing the evidence that was presented to the Refugee Protection Division. Therefore, the matter is remitted to the RPD for redetermination by a differently-constituted panel.
Pursuant to ss. 111(1)(c) of the Act, the Refugee Appeal Division remits the matter for redetermination to the Refugee Protection Division by a differently constituted panel.

This appeal is therefore allowed. (signed) 'Atam Uppal' Atam Uppal January 26, 2015 Date 1 Raza, Syed Masood v. M.C.I (F.C.A., no.
